analysis.one_liner: Halts new mountaintop-removal coal mining permits until federal health studies are finished.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in two House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress after a single subcommittee hearing in June 2022.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would freeze all new permits and permit expansions for mountaintop-removal coal mining — surface mining that uses explosive blasting in the steep slopes of Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, and West Virginia — until the Department of Health and Human Services completes studies on whether the mining harms nearby residents and rules that it poses no health risk. While the studies run, existing mining operations would have to continuously monitor water, air, soil, and noise pollution and post the results publicly, and pay a one-time fee covering the cost of the studies and monitoring.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities near mountaintop-removal mining sites in the four affected states. They would get a stop on new blasting operations while federal scientists determine whether the mining is linked to the elevated rates of birth defects, lung cancer, heart disease, and kidney disease documented in peer-reviewed studies of these counties, plus public access to pollution data from existing mines.

how_it_helps.text: No new mountaintop-removal mining permit or expansion could be issued by the Army Corps of Engineers, EPA, or the Interior Department — or by states — until HHS concludes the mining poses no health risk to surrounding communities [S2][S3].

The National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences would run comprehensive studies of the health effects of mountaintop-removal mining on nearby residents, answering a question the bill's findings say existing peer-reviewed research links to elevated birth defects, hospitalizations, and mortality [S2][S3].

Until the determination is made, operators must continuously monitor water, air, noise, and soil pollution and submit results monthly, which HHS would post in a searchable public database within seven days [S2][S3].
The federal cost of the studies and monitoring would be paid by the mining companies themselves through a one-time fee, not by taxpayers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies conducting mountaintop-removal mining. They would face a moratorium on new permits and expansions until HHS clears the practice, mandatory continuous pollution monitoring, and a one-time fee covering the federal research bill. Workers and towns dependent on new coal mining in the region would bear the indirect cost if the moratorium lasted long or the determination went against the industry.

drawbacks.text: The permit moratorium is open-ended: it lasts until HHS issues a finding, and if the studies take years, no new mine or expansion in the four states could be permitted in the meantime, cutting off mining jobs and coal-company revenue in a region already economically dependent on coal [S3].

The moratorium applies even before the studies reach a conclusion, so it bars a project on the possibility of harm rather than a proven one; an honest supporter has to defend halting an entire regional industry on preliminary evidence [S2][S3].

The health evidence cited in the bill's findings — elevated birth defects, lung cancer, heart and kidney disease — is associational; the bill itself acknowledges the links need federal confirmation, which is the study the moratorium is meant to allow [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill puts the entire burden on one industry and one region while the benefit — cleaner water and air and an answer on a possible health crisis — goes to the people living around the mines. If the suspected health links are real, the trade is heavily in favor of residents; if they are not, the cost is an indefinite freeze on a struggling regional industry. The bill's design addresses that risk by funding the studies quickly with industry fees rather than taxpayer money, but it never got far enough to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2021 and sent to the Natural Resources and Energy and Commerce committees, got one subcommittee hearing in June 2022, and the Congress ended in January 2023 with no committee vote and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Yarmuth of Kentucky introduced the Appalachian Communities Health Emergency Act on March 18, 2021 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee, meaning both would have to act on the parts in their jurisdiction [S5].
Within two days it went to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and in May 2021 to the Natural Resources Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee [S5].
The only action after that was a subcommittee hearing on June 9, 2022; neither committee ever approved the bill and the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies with mountaintop-removal operations in Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, and West Virginia are better off: they faced no permit freeze, no mandatory pollution monitoring, and no fee, and the federal health studies the bill would have ordered never happened.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call shows the split; all five House sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill freezes new permits and expansions until HHS rules the mining poses no health risk, imposes continuous pollution monitoring, and charges a one-time fee to fund the studies. Because the industry's revenue depends on continued blasting that peer-reviewed studies link to elevated disease and mortality in surrounding counties, its interest in defeating the moratorium ran against the health interests of nearby residents.
